title: Shortcuts to Parameter Sweeps
authors: Chi Xiang, Guodong Cheng, Geng Li
abstract: Efficient evaluation of stationary parametric sensitivities over broad parameter ranges is important for identifying influential training data, fitting force fields, and predicting material responses, but standard pointwise approaches require repeated relaxation and sampling. Here we introduce Shortcuts to Parameter Sweeps (STPS), an engineered control strategy that uses an auxiliary control to transport the probability density along a prescribed family of instantaneous stationary states during a finite-time parameter sweep. This enables the continuous response curve over the full parameter interval to be estimated from a single controlled sweep using covariance-based response relations. STPS applies to both equilibrium and nonequilibrium steady-state systems, including those with unknown stationary distributions, and can be implemented directly using stationary samples in high-dimensional settings. Numerical tests on single-particle and interacting many-body systems show that STPS yields response curves in close agreement with reference results. These findings establish STPS as an efficient, sample-based framework for continuous sensitivity analysis in stochastic simulations.
summary: The paper introduces Shortcuts to Parameter Sweeps (STPS), an advanced technique to calculate how system properties change with respect to varying control parameters ($\lambda$). By engineering a controlled trajectory, STPS estimates the entire continuous response curve from just one simulation run. This offers a significant computational advantage over traditional methods that require running many independent simulations.
main_problem: The core challenge is efficiently calculating how stationary expectations (response functions) change when system parameters are varied over a wide range, as standard methods require costly repeated sampling.
main_result: The proposed Shortcuts to Parameter Sweeps (STPS) framework allows estimating the continuous response curve from a single controlled simulation sweep, providing an efficient, sample-based alternative to traditional methods.
method: STPS engineers an auxiliary control field to guide the system's probability density along the instantaneous stationary manifold during one finite-time sweep. This leverages covariance-based response relations derived from transport theory.
model_or_system: The method is general, applicable to both equilibrium and non-equilibrium steady-state systems, including many-body interacting particle models (e.g., trapped or rotating systems).

paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitation of standard methods, develops the theoretical basis linking response to stationary transport equations, details the practical implementation using learned fields (GNNs), and validates the approach by comparing results against established finite difference techniques.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant for studying open quantum systems or many-body dynamics where parameters (like coupling strengths or external driving frequencies) are varied slowly. It provides a computational shortcut to map out parameter landscapes without prohibitive simulation costs.
